The question of whether teething causes fever in babies is a matter of conflicting research findings and expert opinions. Several credible sources state that teething does not cause true clinical fever: [d3] cites Seattle Children's and research indicating "the research does not support this claim (or is at best inconclusive)," and [d6] states "there's no evidence to support teething causes fever." Similarly, [d7] calls the idea "largely a myth," and [d8] explicitly labels it "Teething myth #1: teething causes fevers — This is false." However, other credible sources acknowledge that mild temperature rises may occur: [d9] (NCBI/InformedHealth.org) states "teething can cause a child's body temperature to go up," [d4] (Children's Hospital LA) notes "teething can sometimes cause a very mild, low-grade fever" while clarifying that "higher fevers — 101°F or above — are not caused by teething," and [d5] (Royal Children's Hospital) states "children who are teething may have a fever of up to 38°C," but adds that temperatures above 38°C "should never just be attributed to teething." The most consistent point across sources is that true clinical fever (38°C/100.4°F or higher) during teething is more likely caused by an infection or illness coinciding with the teething period, not by teething itself [d1][d2][d3][d5][d6].
